text: We are an international tobacco and nicotine company. Our principal products are combustible cigarettes, which we sell under the Marlboro, L&M, Chesterfield, Philip Morris, Bond Street and Parliament brands, and smoke-free products, which include heated tobacco units, oral nicotine pouches and e-vapour products. Combustible cigarettes accounted for 61.4% of our net revenues in 2025 and were shipped to consumers in more than 170 markets outside the United States. We manufacture cigarettes at 38 owned facilities and purchase tobacco leaf from suppliers in 27 countries. Our stated ambition is to increase the share of net revenues from smoke-free products, and we continue to invest in heated tobacco capacity, but we expect combustible cigarettes to remain a majority of our net revenues and the substantial majority of our shipment volume for the foreseeable future. Our business is subject to excise taxation, advertising restrictions, graphic health warning requirements, flavour bans and, in a growing number of markets, generational sales prohibitions.

Our products contain nicotine, which is addictive, and the use of our combustible products causes serious disease. Regulatory authorities in many of our markets have adopted or are considering measures that would further restrict the sale, packaging, flavouring or nicotine content of our products, including prohibitions on sales to anyone born after a specified year. Litigation and regulatory action of this kind could materially reduce our shipment volume and net revenues. Public health bodies, institutional investors and a growing number of asset owners apply exclusion policies that prevent them from holding securities issued by tobacco manufacturers, which may reduce demand for our shares and increase our cost of capital. We also face reputational risk from allegations that our marketing reaches young adults, from the conduct of distributors in markets where we do not control the retail channel, and from illicit trade in counterfeit versions of our brands.

Legal proceedings covering a wide range of matters are pending or threatened against us and our subsidiaries in various jurisdictions. These include smoking and health class actions in Canada, individual smoking and health claims in Brazil, Argentina, Italy and Nigeria, and health care cost recovery actions brought by provincial governments. In the Canadian proceedings, companies including our subsidiary Rothmans, Benson & Hedges Inc. remain subject to a court-supervised creditor protection process following judgments in the Blais and Letourneau class actions. We recorded a charge of $482 million in the fourth quarter of 2025 in connection with these matters. An adverse outcome in any pending smoking and health proceeding could require us to pay damages that are material to our consolidated results of operations and cash flows, and we cannot predict the outcome of the appeals that remain outstanding.

Campaigners have accused the tobacco industry of using music festivals, influencer partnerships and branded lounges to put nicotine pouches in front of young adults in lower-income markets where advertising rules are weaker. Researchers who reviewed 1,400 social media posts said roughly a third carried no health warning and that the accounts posting them had a median follower age under 30. Philip Morris International said its marketing is aimed only at adults who already smoke or use nicotine, that it audits its agencies, and that it supports age verification at the point of sale. A spokesperson for a coalition of health charities said exclusion lists are the only tool trustees can rely on, because company-level assurances cannot be audited by investors from the outside. Health ministers in two of the markets named in the report have asked their regulators to review whether pouch advertising falls inside existing tobacco advertising bans.

Philip Morris International raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook after heated tobacco unit shipments rose 11.2% year on year in the second quarter, and now expects currency-neutral adjusted diluted earnings per share growth of 10% to 12%. Smoke-free products reached 40.3% of net revenues in the quarter. Combustible cigarette shipment volume fell 1.4%, a smaller decline than the company guided to in April, helped by pricing in Turkey, Indonesia and Egypt. The company reaffirmed its dividend and said it expects to complete its current capacity expansion in Europe by the end of 2027.

Health ministers from eleven countries issued a joint statement calling for nicotine pouches to be regulated on the same footing as combustible tobacco, including bans on flavours other than tobacco and mandatory plain packaging. The statement cites rising use among people aged 18 to 24 and says voluntary industry marketing codes have not prevented products from being promoted to that group. Industry representatives said the products help adult smokers switch away from cigarettes and that treating them identically to cigarettes removes that incentive.
